items.title: Epic Dunks On Steam With Vibe-Coded Storefront And Gets Roasted: ‘This Launcher Is So F*cking Vibeslopped Its Funny’
items.author: Ethan Gach
items.summary: The Epic Games Store needs a pick-me-up. Eight years in, the glorified Fortnite launcher is great for getting free games but has languished amid the company’s
items.text:
The Epic Games Store needs a pick-me-up. Eight years in, the glorified Fortnite launcher is great for getting free games but has languished amid the company’s other priorities. A plan to overhaul the storefront was revealed a few months ago and it was basically to make it more like Steam. Now Epic Games has revealed that improvements will also be vibe-coded with AI.

“Programming is hard,” the company wrote in its official announcement post for a newly released preview version of a revamped launcher for the store. “So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that’s way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look. This first release is light on features. Think of it as a speedboat and not a yacht! Though it does have advanced digital commerce technology such as a shopping cart.”

Yes, posting rage-bait appears to be part of the strategy here. Just a week after forcing internal game developers to go “AI first” and incorporate genAI even into their artwork pipelines, Epic is embracing the tech publicly as well teasing upcoming changes to the place where it wants millions of players to store their credit card info. The company even took shots at Steam.

“We vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy,” the Epic X account posted. “Don’t believe us? Test it out for yourself in Preview.” It was accompanied by a graphic showing that the genAI storefront performed faster on certain responsiveness benchmarks than Valve’s competitor. This isn’t just a stunt or a flex for AI boosters on Elon Musk’s social media platform, though. The adults at Epic aren’t joking about wanting to make its storefront more appealing.

“It’s been rebuilt entirely from the ground up,” Epic Games Store general manager Martin Keely told IGN. “So this is a completely new tech stack, a complete new rewrite of both the shell, which has the download manager, library, and the app itself, as well as the new store architecture. So features like discover and product detail pages, those have all been rewritten.”

But the effect online has been a wave of people roasting Epic’s “vibe-coded” framing of the rollout and the fact that the launcher appears borked in ways not usually seen for a product rollout users are expected to take seriously.

Epic also announced that it’s bringing Fortnite to Linux via Proton, a compatibility layer made by, surprise, Valve. “Bold of them to sh*t on Valve/Steam, and then literally use Proton internally for Windows compat on Linux…,” one VR modder wrote on X. “This launcher is so fucking vibeslopped its funny, but holy crap, these people are hilarious.” A Twitch streamer wrote in the comments beneath Epic’s announcement, “Are you seriously incapable of embarrassment? I’m not leaving Steam for this trash.”

Epic CEO Tim Sweeney confirmed this week that Epic is “retool[ing] for maximum AI acceleration.” “The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal,” he added. The proof will be in what the company actually ships. Its Epic overhaul preview has yet to pass the test of “more” or “better.” “The new Epic Games Launcher is in Preview for testing, and with any beta there could be issues,” reads the disclaimer. Epic promises those problems won’t affect players once they actually boot up their games, most of which weren’t vibe-coded. At least for now.

items.title: "We are here to give you something to believe in": the former Disco Elysium devs of Summer Eternal reveal new RPG Red Rooster, a game of fire, water and alternate selves
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: Earlier this month, the former Disco Elysium developers of worker co-operative studio Summer Eternal sent me a 500-page anthology describing their new game Red
items.text:
Earlier this month, the former Disco Elysium developers of worker co-operative studio Summer Eternal sent me a 500-page anthology describing their new game Red Rooster. It's a 3D, real-time, third-person RPG you could broadly style as a spiritual Disco successor, working in the tradition of Planescape: Torment and Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines, but which also owes much inspiration to Baldur's Gate 3 and Dark Messiah of Might and Magic. It takes place in a magic realist, "our-world-adjacent", mightily flammable and divided river city called Arta-Tantor, created with Unreal Engine and housing a "physics-powered sandbox of objects you can individually move, manipulate – and burn."

Here, you will live out the story of Redrick Roost, a convict serving a life sentence after accidentally rendering thousands of people catatonic by means of an "auto-meditation" headset. Much like Disco's Harry, Redrick has a whole world of characters in his head – a hallucinatory vacuum shop or "chicken coop" full of alternate selves or "roosters", who vie for dominance as the game goes on, affecting your dialogue options and abilities. Redrick's broad goal, having been recruited by government spooks, is to identify the arsonist working at a fire station run by his own hero brother. You've got a week to pull this off before your parole hearing. Your colleagues include Dr Astrid Albers, a mathematician with an opiate problem who wakes up one day to find that mathematics has Gone Wrong.

Much like that last paragraph, the Summer Eternal book is a dense, knotty, wild-eyed thing. It's divided into two parts. The first is an account of Summer Eternal's formation that aims to situate the new studio within (and often, against) today's videogame industry and culture. There are essays on aesthetics, generative AI and the difficulty of pursuing anti-capitalist game development while being obliged to compromise a little for the sake of funding. There are open-ended interviews with several well-known game developers, including former BioWare devs Mark Darrah and David Gaider, together with sci-fi novelist Ted Chiang, Marxist economist Richard Wolff, and union organisers at United Videogame Workers-CWA. Also, a chat with those scruffy apparatchiks at indie journalist outfit Aftermath... and an acknowledgements page in which Summer Eternal thank myself and Mark Warren for our previous online coverage of the studio's founding. Look, we hacks have got to get some limelight now and then.

The book is further evidence that Summer Eternal are the most Marxist of the post-Disco studios. Put it this way: there is a double-page spread in which the eponymous red rooster is pictured striking down the vulture of venture capitalism, while studio founder and former ZA/UM narrative designer/principal writer Dora Klindžić decries "bourgeois virgins who administrate their battles from office desks".

At the risk of being branded a bourgeois virgin, I do think that Marxist writers can always benefit from some tactical self-deprecation – Disco Elysium was very good at seeing the funny side, and still had teeth as a political document. Still, this is a manifesto for a studio, not a piece of fiction, and I genuinely got a bit tearful about Klindžić's visions for a studio run for the benefit of workers and artists, in a universe that is being strangled by finance and cannibalised by LLMs. "We are preparing a conflagration, an end to mourning, an end to the poison fog of demoralization and the apathy tears of the mentally imprisoned," she writes. "With charred fingers, we are here to give you something to hope for. We are here to give you something to believe in."

More specifically, they are here to give us an RPG. The second half of the book is a massive pitch document and lore bible for Red Rooster, a game that is in the "early pre-production phase", with 3-4 years to go before release... providing Summer Eternal can pull together the funding. Obviously, the funding situation is a concern: I'd like to write more about the studio's structure, which divides shares between creatives and investors with a small portion set aside for fans. In the meantime, I'll say that Red Rooster sounds fascinating.

The section on Red Rooster opens with a lengthy fictional university essay about the history of Arta-Tantor, which is sort of three cities or "member-territories" nested close together - the result of centuries of war, rivalry and overseas exploitation with a broad theme of fire vs water. The city's factions include groups of heavily armed game wardens and couriers, together with a long-suffering fire service that originally consisted of slaves, and is now a mix of professionals, amateurs, and prisoners doing community service. Another, redacted in-world memorandum hints at a psionic organisation of some kind.

And then there's the cast. The book tells you a lot about Redrick and Astrid, including some details I'd rather you discover for yourself. Redrick's history is complicated, to say the least. His parents died in a house fire. At the age of 12, he was seduced by a school science teacher, who was later imprisoned not for statutory rape but commandeering a postal vehicle. As an adult, he fell in with the inventor of the aforesaid "auto-meditation" device, who capitalised on the infamy created by his "affair" for marketing purposes.

When the Baku headset malfunctioned, inducing "mass mental fracturing", it also gave rise to the Coop, Redrick's eerie inner sanctum, which is modelled after the vacuum shop he once worked in. Here, you'll spend XP to modify your build, while interacting with various Rooster-selves, who may form factions as they seek to dominate one another and shape Redrick's overall persona. Possible Roosters include a "Rooster-Raconteur" who can't stop debating people, a pathological gambler, and an "Overkompensaaator" who wears sunglasses indoors. More Roosters will appear as the game goes on, and you'll get to decide whether to admit, strengthen, and repress them to alter Redrick's stats and dialogue options, similar to the Copotypes in Disco Elysium. "Repression" is an actual dice-driven encounter, with several potential outcomes besides victory and failure. It's also possible for repressed or rejected Roosters to push through and hijack the Coop, if you continue to behave in a way that leans into their archetype.

Redrick's initial companion character Astrid, a maths prodigy working at a local research institute, isn't quite as messy, but she isn't exactly Miles Tails Prower either. She teams up with him after being caught overdosing on opiates and forced into a state-supervised rehabilitation program. Her job is to keep an eye on Redrick while he searches for the aforesaid arsonist. In the book, Astrid is defined by her claustrophobic relationship with her overbearing novelist father, her tendency to lie, and her realisation, one day, that the laws of mathematics have somehow altered, right down to the bones of the prime number system – an event that might have something to do with an on-going heatwave.

There is much to say about Astrid, but all I'll add for the moment is that her visual inspirations include Patti Smith and Gollum. She has stage presence for lightyears, while Redrick is characterised as earnest and apologetic and not-quite-there. Redrick can bolster his look using a rhizomatic clothing system where you set up fashion synergies on a grid, rather than the usual equipment screen in which clothing is categorised by body part.

If these characters are absolutely the kind of people you'd expect to meet in Disco Elysium, Red Rooster cleaves from that inspiration with its unhealthy interest in physics. There's a chapter in the book where game director Argo Tuulik frames the game's manipulable object world as a key point of differentiation: "this visceral connection, developed through a myriad of small interactions that form the all-encompassing connective tissue, is the holy grail. The missing physical counterpart to the ultra-reactive psychological role-play. The logical next step in the RPG genre. It is the most important pillar of Red Rooster."

The game will, amongst other things, allow you to lob and break objects with different weight, fragility and elasticity, from chairs to bike tyres. A "simplified but realistic real-time fire simulation" plays out Redrick's torturous relationship with fire, spreading between surfaces according to material properties: by the sounds of things, acts of arson are how you'll pursue particular subplots and revelations, though not everything in the world can burn.

The world is also subject to change and entropy, independent of your activities: lightbulbs will burn out, falling leaves will cover staircases, trash bags will be emptied, local sculptors will slowly turn hunks of stone into statues. These unfolding phenomena sit within a web of 'terrain factors' imposed by Arta-Trantor's weird tripartite political culture, with a "topologically complex map where international borders criss-cross the streets, bisect buildings and bedroms, and create enclaves and counter-enclaves within the same neighbourhoods".

The devs say you'll move across a multitude of "soft borders" as you explore, which creates bizarre possibilities and constraints. You might cross a street to move into a different jurisdiction and thereby throw off a cop. You might cross a bar when the clock strikes 10pm to carry on drinking in a territory where it's legal to sell booze until 2am. Or you might have to make use of a window to get around a revised border policy, rather than opening the front door.

I'll end by stressing that Summer Eternal is still far more pitch for a game than a game. Much of the above may change, and the developers make no secret of the fact that they're still raising funds. I'm especially keen on all the hypnotic rhetoric around fire, as somebody who's written a bit here and there about procedural fire systems in videogames. I'll likely be diving back into the book for more stories. In the meantime, you can order a copy yourself via the official website.

blocks.x: Earlier this month, the former Disco Elysium developers of worker co-operative studio Summer Eternal sent me a 500-page anthology describing their new game Red Rooster. It's a 3D, real-time, third-person RPG you could broadly style as a spiritual Disco successor, working in the tradition of Planescape: Torment and Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines, but which also owes much inspiration to Baldur's Gate 3 and Dark Messiah of Might and Magic. It takes place in a magic realist, "our-world-adjacent", mightily flammable and divided river city called Arta-Tantor, created with Unreal Engine and housing a "physics-powered sandbox of objects you can individually move, manipulate – and burn."

Here, you will live out the story of Redrick Roost, a convict serving a life sentence after accidentally rendering thousands of people catatonic by means of an "auto-meditation" headset. Much like Disco's Harry, Redrick has a whole world of characters in his head – a hallucinatory vacuum shop or "chicken coop" full of alternate selves or "roosters", who vie for dominance as the game goes on, affecting your dialogue options and abilities. Redrick's broad goal, having been recruited by government spooks, is to identify the arsonist working at a fire station run by his own hero brother. You've got a week to pull this off before your parole hearing. Your colleagues include Dr Astrid Albers, a mathematician with an opiate problem who wakes up one day to find that mathematics has Gone Wrong.

Much like that last paragraph, the Summer Eternal book is a dense, knotty, wild-eyed thing. It's divided into two parts. The first is an account of Summer Eternal's formation that aims to situate the new studio within (and often, against) today's videogame industry and culture. There are essays on aesthetics, generative AI and the difficulty of pursuing anti-capitalist game development while being obliged to compromise a little for the sake of funding. There are open-ended interviews with several well-known game developers, including former BioWare devs Mark Darrah and David Gaider, together with sci-fi novelist Ted Chiang, Marxist economist Richard Wolff, and union organisers at United Videogame Workers-CWA. Also, a chat with those scruffy apparatchiks at indie journalist outfit Aftermath... and an acknowledgements page in which Summer Eternal thank myself and Mark Warren for our previous online coverage of the studio's founding. Look, we hacks have got to get some limelight now and then.

The book is further evidence that Summer Eternal are the most Marxist of the post-Disco studios. Put it this way: there is a double-page spread in which the eponymous red rooster is pictured striking down the vulture of venture capitalism, while studio founder and former ZA/UM narrative designer/principal writer Dora Klindžić decries "bourgeois virgins who administrate their battles from office desks".

At the risk of being branded a bourgeois virgin, I do think that Marxist writers can always benefit from some tactical self-deprecation – Disco Elysium was very good at seeing the funny side, and still had teeth as a political document. Still, this is a manifesto for a studio, not a piece of fiction, and I genuinely got a bit tearful about Klindžić's visions for a studio run for the benefit of workers and artists, in a universe that is being strangled by finance and cannibalised by LLMs. "We are preparing a conflagration, an end to mourning, an end to the poison fog of demoralization and the apathy tears of the mentally imprisoned," she writes. "With charred fingers, we are here to give you something to hope for. We are here to give you something to believe in."

More specifically, they are here to give us an RPG. The second half of the book is a massive pitch document and lore bible for Red Rooster, a game that is in the "early pre-production phase", with 3-4 years to go before release... providing Summer Eternal can pull together the funding. Obviously, the funding situation is a concern: I'd like to write more about the studio's structure, which divides shares between creatives and investors with a small portion set aside for fans. In the meantime, I'll say that Red Rooster sounds fascinating.

The section on Red Rooster opens with a lengthy fictional university essay about the history of Arta-Tantor, which is sort of three cities or "member-territories" nested close together - the result of centuries of war, rivalry and overseas exploitation with a broad theme of fire vs water. The city's factions include groups of heavily armed game wardens and couriers, together with a long-suffering fire service that originally consisted of slaves, and is now a mix of professionals, amateurs, and prisoners doing community service. Another, redacted in-world memorandum hints at a psionic organisation of some kind.

And then there's the cast. The book tells you a lot about Redrick and Astrid, including some details I'd rather you discover for yourself. Redrick's history is complicated, to say the least. His parents died in a house fire. At the age of 12, he was seduced by a school science teacher, who was later imprisoned not for statutory rape but commandeering a postal vehicle. As an adult, he fell in with the inventor of the aforesaid "auto-meditation" device, who capitalised on the infamy created by his "affair" for marketing purposes.

When the Baku headset malfunctioned, inducing "mass mental fracturing", it also gave rise to the Coop, Redrick's eerie inner sanctum, which is modelled after the vacuum shop he once worked in. Here, you'll spend XP to modify your build, while interacting with various Rooster-selves, who may form factions as they seek to dominate one another and shape Redrick's overall persona. Possible Roosters include a "Rooster-Raconteur" who can't stop debating people, a pathological gambler, and an "Overkompensaaator" who wears sunglasses indoors. More Roosters will appear as the game goes on, and you'll get to decide whether to admit, strengthen, and repress them to alter Redrick's stats and dialogue options, similar to the Copotypes in Disco Elysium. "Repression" is an actual dice-driven encounter, with several potential outcomes besides victory and failure. It's also possible for repressed or rejected Roosters to push through and hijack the Coop, if you continue to behave in a way that leans into their archetype.

Redrick's initial companion character Astrid, a maths prodigy working at a local research institute, isn't quite as messy, but she isn't exactly Miles Tails Prower either. She teams up with him after being caught overdosing on opiates and forced into a state-supervised rehabilitation program. Her job is to keep an eye on Redrick while he searches for the aforesaid arsonist. In the book, Astrid is defined by her claustrophobic relationship with her overbearing novelist father, her tendency to lie, and her realisation, one day, that the laws of mathematics have somehow altered, right down to the bones of the prime number system – an event that might have something to do with an on-going heatwave.

There is much to say about Astrid, but all I'll add for the moment is that her visual inspirations include Patti Smith and Gollum. She has stage presence for lightyears, while Redrick is characterised as earnest and apologetic and not-quite-there. Redrick can bolster his look using a rhizomatic clothing system where you set up fashion synergies on a grid, rather than the usual equipment screen in which clothing is categorised by body part.

If these characters are absolutely the kind of people you'd expect to meet in Disco Elysium, Red Rooster cleaves from that inspiration with its unhealthy interest in physics. There's a chapter in the book where game director Argo Tuulik frames the game's manipulable object world as a key point of differentiation: "this visceral connection, developed through a myriad of small interactions that form the all-encompassing connective tissue, is the holy grail. The missing physical counterpart to the ultra-reactive psychological role-play. The logical next step in the RPG genre. It is the most important pillar of Red Rooster."

The game will, amongst other things, allow you to lob and break objects with different weight, fragility and elasticity, from chairs to bike tyres. A "simplified but realistic real-time fire simulation" plays out Redrick's torturous relationship with fire, spreading between surfaces according to material properties: by the sounds of things, acts of arson are how you'll pursue particular subplots and revelations, though not everything in the world can burn.

The world is also subject to change and entropy, independent of your activities: lightbulbs will burn out, falling leaves will cover staircases, trash bags will be emptied, local sculptors will slowly turn hunks of stone into statues. These unfolding phenomena sit within a web of 'terrain factors' imposed by Arta-Trantor's weird tripartite political culture, with a "topologically complex map where international borders criss-cross the streets, bisect buildings and bedroms, and create enclaves and counter-enclaves within the same neighbourhoods".

The devs say you'll move across a multitude of "soft borders" as you explore, which creates bizarre possibilities and constraints. You might cross a street to move into a different jurisdiction and thereby throw off a cop. You might cross a bar when the clock strikes 10pm to carry on drinking in a territory where it's legal to sell booze until 2am. Or you might have to make use of a window to get around a revised border policy, rather than opening the front door.

items.title: 'AI godfather' worries we're creating 'alien beings' with artificial intelligence, with pesky moral implications
items.author: Jess Kinghorn

items.text:
Geoffrey Hinton is a computer scientist known for his foundational work in AI, specifically when it comes to neural networks (ie, approaching machine-learning a bit like our fleshy brain-learning). As such, he's been described as the 'AI godfather'. But, perhaps surprisingly, he recently described AI as "alien beings" that humans have a "moral obligation" towards.

"We’re creating alien beings—meaning we’re not the only intelligent beings around," He said in a recent interview with The Guardian, "And the reality is, we only have a couple of years to adapt to that.”

Hinton claims, "AI models understand what they’re saying. You couldn’t possibly answer all the questions without understanding the question. It’s ridiculous to say they don’t understand.”

Now, far be it for me to argue with an expert in the field, but I feel like 'understanding' is doing a lot of heavy lifting here. For just one thing, I'm not sure an 'answer' consisting of what is statistically most likely to follow a prompted question is really 'understanding.' In other words, I don't have a Nobel Prize laureate like Hinton does, but I am at least familiar with the Chinese Room thought experiment.

Hinton also says, "The reality is, we’re making beings of a different kind. And the big tech companies keep saying: we want it smarter. This is crazy. We should care as much about all the other aspects of a being as you do about its intelligence.”

A close up of the vacant expression of Meta's Muse AI mascot, Jolly. (Image credit: Meta)AI regulation and 'alignment' (ie, training AI to have the same goals and values as humans) have been hot button issues lately. For instance, the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident is not yet a small dot in the rearview mirror, and the president of Microsoft claims that a carton of milk is more regulated than AI.

Hinton cut his ties to Google in 2023 in order to "freely speak out about the risks of AI," and he's sceptical about the AI industry's attempts to self-regulate. He quips, "Do we think tobacco companies should have been allowed to design the warnings on the packets? So that they could print them in a six-point font, in dark grey on black?"

Even so, Hinton also expresses concerns about the path to AI regulation, saying that humans bear a moral obligation towards AI models.

"Once you start talking about, ‘We have a moral obligation towards these alien beings,’ you lose your audience. I’ve struggled with this issue," Hinton says, "We care about people. [But] we’re making these things and there’s nothing to stop us giving these things—which are more intelligent than us—less rights than us. I’m willing to be selfish and choose human beings. Of course, we should try to make them so that they’re very happy in a symbiotic relationship with us, where our concerns are weighed more heavily than their concerns."

The face of a robot in Atomic Heart. (Image credit: Mundfish)Hinton argues, “People have a very bad model of what people are, and that’s why they fail to understand how these AI models are very like us. Most people don’t understand what consciousness is. They don’t understand what subjective experience is, and they’re very confident that even though they don’t understand it, they’re sure AI doesn’t have it.”

While I'm not a doctor of Philosophy myself, I do know someone who is—our very own Jacob Fox. He's already shared his thoughts on the subject of 'AI consciousness' here, and I asked him for his insight again on this story.

The face of an AI in Prove You're Human. (Image credit: Sunset Visitor)Jacob told me he did not agree with Hinton's moral obligation argument, going on to write more broadly, "While it's good that Hinton is acknowledging subjective experience is relevant to consciousness, he hasn't given a single good reason why we should take seriously the idea that AI has it. And when we interpret personhood as to do with objective characteristics such as rationality, behaviour, and so on, rather than experience, we run the risk of ascribing moral and legal and political weight to them. Which runs the risk of giving AI companies a massive moral argument to keep the industry going, despite how it affects actual humans."

To put it another way, the industry argument for AI consciousness or AI rights is not an altruistic one—it is arguably a cynical tactic to continue business as usual.

items.title: Players Are Furious About Total War: Shogun 2‘s AI-Upscaled ‘Enhanced’ Edition
items.author: John Walker
items.summary: October 13 saw the release of Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition, described as being “the updated, enhanced, and complete version of the grand strategy
items.text:
October 13 saw the release of Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition, described as being “the updated, enhanced, and complete version of the grand strategy classic.” Players are describing it as “literally the greed they talk about in the bible,” with 82 percent negative reviews over the last 24 hours.

Originally released in 2011, Total War: Shogun 2 was received with widespread jubilation. Routinely scoring 9s and 10s across the board, it was heralded as the best game in the already very healthy Total War series, and has remained one of the most highly rated games in the franchise since. In 2019, Kotaku rated it the very best of the lot, and The Gamer more recently put it at #2, behind only the then-just-released Three Kingdoms. The point is, people love this game. A re-release, designed to run on modern machines, should have been an absolute gimme.

Instead, the new version is currently firmly in the Overwhelmingly Negative position on Steam, being slammed for crummy performance, bugs old and new, broken mod support, a litany of graphical issues, and the alleged (and undisclosed) use of AI upscaling for the game’s unit cards. That Sega has chosen to delist all the previous versions of the game from Steam at the same time, and increase the price for this new version, is only making people more furious. Which is in stark contrast the extremely few press reviews the game has received, with just four critics giving it a Metascore of 86.

A new generation

Running the game certainly feels crummy, the camera movement jagged and the art this peculiar mishmash of old and slightly less old, looking blurry and dated and certainly not attractive. It certainly doesn’t look modern.

We’ve reached out to Creative Assembly to ask about AI use, but have yet to hear anything back. But given there’s no declaration on the Steam page, it does make some of the game’s art pretty tricky to explain. I’ve gone through the new game’s encyclopedia and compared some of the images to those in the original, and…it’s not good. Below you can see some comparisons, the original version on the left and the new version on the right.

You can see how the process has confused the central wooden bar on the top deck of the boat for part of the background, and so smooshed one of the figures to death, along with the loss of coherent detail in many areas, including the bow strings. If it’s not genAI then it’s inexplicable, and even if it is, it remains incredibly sloppy work.

Here’s another that emphasizes some really crappy consequences of this.

Obviously it look significantly worse, not least where the AI hasn’t understood the plumes of smoke from gunshots and rendered them as, I dunno, lampshades. But more egregious are the flags, where the specific emblem of the unit type is lost, now displayed as a sort of art-deco jellyfish. Also, check out the guy at the front up top, who has gone from standing on the far side to now inserted between two slats of wood.

But by far my favorite so far is General’s Hatamoto, where the upscaling has not coped with the scant details in the original’s depiction of the face below the helmet, and instead decided to merge the two into some sort of 16th-century automaton.

The lack of an AI declaration on the Steam page violates Valve’s rules, so expect to see that added in a hurry. And hopefully we’ll soon hear from the developers, so we can find out which version of the familiar “Placeholder art was created using generative AI and was unfortunately included in the final release” excuse we get.

Published Oct 15, 2026, 5:46 AM EDT

Tom Wilson is a Gaming Features Writer at Screen Rant. Over the past five years, Tom has worked as the Editor-in-Chief at The Game Crater, as a Staff Writer for GamingIntel, a List Writer at TheGamer, and, of course, as a Senior Writer at ScreenRant. Tom has experience writing reviews, guides, news, and features, and has been responsible for teams of writers, training them and editing their work.
Tom graduated with a Masters in Multimedia Journalism, and has since gone on to build up his portfolio of games journalism work.

Xbox will not be getting one of 2026's Game of the Year contenders as a direct consequence of an ongoing boycott of Microsoft. This has been officially confirmed by the game's developer, which spoke out in a social media post after being questioned about the missing Xbox port of its recently released and critically acclaimed 2026 game. This is not a fan-led boycott, but an official boycott against Microsoft itself, something that the developer is actively in support of.

The news comes amid a series of controversies surrounding Xbox, which is currently attempting to restore the goodwill its brand name once carried through the implementation of new leadership and a focus on first-party exclusives. While Game Pass continues to be stuffed with first-party titles, day-one releases, and assorted third-party games, the loss of this 2026 GOTY contender is sure to disappoint fans, although its developer hopes they'll understand while the boycott is still ongoing.

The 2026 critically acclaimed title Big Walk proved to be a massive success when its developer, the Australian Studio House House, launched it back in August. It offers fans an expansive open-world co-op experience unlike anything else, which, amid the rise of what is being affectionately called "friendslop", proved to be a winning formula for many. Its surreal landscapes, clever puzzle design, and use of proximity chat created an experience that many believe is in with a chance of winning the coveted Game of the Year award, as well as a respectable score of 91 on Metacritic.

Big Walk was released on PS Plus, PS5, Nintendo Switch 2, and PC, with House House opting to skip Xbox. It has now transpired that the reason for forgoing an Xbox port is a direct consequence of the developer supporting the Palestine-led BDS (Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions) boycott. The movement, which has been ongoing since 2005, aims to "pressure Israel to comply with international law" by "effectively challenging international support for Israeli apartheid and settler-colonialism," according to its official website.

In a statement posted to House House's official X account, the developer stated that it would not be releasing an Xbox port of Big Walk until "Microsoft and/or XBOX have been removed as BDS boycott targets." Microsoft is one of the priority targets for the BDS movement, with its website calling it "the most complicit tech company in Israel’s illegal apartheid regime and ongoing genocide against 2.3 million Palestinians in Gaza." House House explained that it believed that "meaningful change can be made in the world," stating:

“In June 2026 we announced that the release of Big Walk would be limited to computers, Switch 2, and PS5. Since then, we have received many messages and comments, asking about a future XBOX release. We would like to address those questions here. We have made the decision not to release Big Walk on XBOX, in accordance with the Palestinian-led BDS movement’s call to boycott Microsoft, and their designation of Microsoft Games (and XBOX) as a priority boycott target [...] We’ve made this decision with the belief that meaningful change can be made in the world, that coordinated collective action can confront even the most powerful interests, and that one day, Palestine will be free."

The BDS' boycott against Microsoft is ongoing and unlikely to end any time soon. It cites Microsoft's involvement with the Israeli military, the extent of which was revealed by a recent joint investigation by The Guardian, the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, and Local Call. items.text:
Russell Crowe’s Best-Reviewed Movie in 27 Years Officially Removed From 1,500 Theaters

Vertical Entertainment / Courtesy Everett Collection

Two new movies featuring Russell Crowe were released in September, and ironically, the one that received worse reviews turned out to be the bigger hit. Both films are two-handers, with Crowe sharing the screen with Jacob Tremblay in his hit Netflix film, and with Ethan Hawke in his theatrical underperformer. The Oscar-winner played a Harvard professor who conducted scientific experiments on a young Ted Kaczynski in Unabomber, which has amassed more than 50 million views so far. The psychological drama holds a poor 25% score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes. Crowe's theatrical release, on the other hand, has emerged as his best-reviewed movie since 1999.

A Western drama that premiered at the Sundance Film Festival earlier this year, the movie grossed around $3.5 million in its domestic run. This puts it in the very bottom tier of Crowe's films. While the actor has certainly experienced major box-office success in his career, he has spent the last decade or so starring in relatively smaller-scale films. A few of them, like the World War II drama Nuremberg and the horror movie The Pope's Exorcist, were able to break out at the box office and deliver solid results. Most of Crowe's recent films, however, have found an audience only after debuting on the home-video market.

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
Which Western Icon Are You Most Like?
No Name · Doc Holliday · Wyatt Earp · Mattie Ross

Pick your name, your gun, your horse and how you spend a night in town, and we will tell you which legend of the Old West you would have been. Four icons are waiting at the end of this: the stranger who never gives his name, the gambler who would die for a friend, the lawman who never wanted the badge, and the girl nobody has ever talked out of anything.

🚬No Name(Dollars Trilogy)

🃏Doc Holliday(Tombstone)

⭐Wyatt Earp(Tombstone)

🐎Mattie Ross(True Grit)

FIND YOUR ICON →

01

The town is about to learn your name. What do they call you?
In a Western, what people call you is already half the character.

AThey never do find it out, so the stranger will have to do.
BA nickname I picked up at a card table and never shook off.
CMarshal, and most people say it with a bit of respect.
DMy full name, and I will correct anybody who tries to shorten it.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

What are you carrying?
Everything out here is character, right down to what is sitting on your hip.

AOne revolver I have had for years and have never once talked about.
BA pistol, a knife and a deck of cards, and the cards do most of the damage.
CA shotgun, because it tends to end arguments rather than start them.
DMy father's gun, which is far too big for me, and I am carrying it anyway.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

What are you riding?
A hero and their horse is one of the oldest relationships in cinema.

ASomething plain that nobody in town would look at twice.
BWhatever I won last night, which may not be strictly mine yet.
CA big steady horse that will not spook when things get loud.
DA pony I overpaid for and named myself, and I will hear nothing against him.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

You have got one evening in town. How does it go?
The saloon is where these films quietly tell you who somebody really is.

AOne drink at the far end of the bar with my back to the wall.
BAt the card table, holding court, up forty dollars and climbing.
CA quick drink, then a walk round town to see that everything is quiet.
DUpstairs with the ledger, working out exactly what tomorrow is going to cost.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

A stranger offers you money for a job that sounds like trouble.
Somebody always turns up with a full purse and a bad idea.

AI ask how much, and then I ask for a good deal more than that.
BI say yes before he has finished, mostly because it sounds like a story.
CI ask him who gets hurt if I turn him down.
DI ask for the terms in writing before anybody shakes on anything.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Somebody is waiting for you in the street. What does the town see?
Two people, an empty road, and everybody else watching from behind the shutters.

ASomebody walking out very slowly who has not said a single word.
BSomebody grinning, which everyone watching finds deeply unnerving.
CSomebody making one last attempt to talk the other man down.
DSomebody far too young to be out there, walking out regardless.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

What is the one thing you will not do out here?
The code is about the only thing west of the river that actually holds.

AExplain myself to somebody who has not earned an explanation.
BRide off and leave a friend standing out there on his own.
CLet a whole town pay for a fight it had nothing to do with.
DLet a grown man tell me I am too young to be standing here.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

The job is finished. Where does the story leave you?
Eight questions in, this is the one that decides your icon.

AOn a ridge somewhere, riding away, without saying goodbye to anybody.
BSomewhere warm and worn out, having enjoyed very nearly all of it.
CHome, with the badge on the table and the whole thing behind me.
DOlder, changed by it, and telling this story for the rest of my life.

REVEAL MY ICON →

The Dust Has Settled
Your Western Icon Is…

Four icons and four completely different ways of walking into trouble.
This is the one you would have been out there, why it fits, and what it would have cost you.

The Dollars Trilogy · 1964–1966

The Man With No Name

You have never explained yourself and you have never needed to,
because people work out fairly quickly that you are the most capable person in the room
without you ever having to mention it.

Eastwood built the character out of everything he refused to do, stripping away the
backstory, the speeches and every bit of reassurance until only the competence was left.

You keep your own counsel, and while other people occasionally find that unnerving, you
have never felt any real need to fix it for them.

The Dollars films work because he genuinely is in it for himself right up until the
moment he is not, and he never explains that part either.

You would be gone before anybody got a chance to thank you.

Doc Holliday · Tombstone · 1993

Doc Holliday

You are the funniest person in most rooms and the most loyal
person in all of them, and you would be genuinely insulted if somebody suggested those two
things were in any tension.

Doc has no real reason to be in this fight beyond the fact that his friend is in it,
which is the only reason he has ever needed for anything.

You lead with wit, and it does a very effective job of hiding how seriously you take the
handful of people you actually care about.

Val Kilmer's performance is the most quoted in the entire genre because the jokes keep
getting sharper as the situation gets worse.

You would spend everything you had on this and still describe it as a good week.

Wyatt Earp · Tombstone · 1993

Wyatt Earp

You never wanted this job, and you took it anyway because the
alternative was standing there watching somebody less careful do it badly, which is the most
Western reason there has ever been.

Earp is the reluctant authority figure, a man who came to town specifically to be left
alone and somehow ended up answerable for all of it.

You are protective by instinct, so when something goes wrong your first thought is who
is exposed rather than who is to blame.

These films understand that keeping order costs far more than breaking it, and that the
person holding the line almost never gets thanked.

You would do the whole thing again, and you would complain about it the entire time.

Mattie Ross · True Grit · 1969 & 2010

Mattie Ross

Nobody has ever successfully talked you out of something you had
already decided was right, and a long line of grown adults has found that out the hard way.

Mattie is the most relentless character in the Western canon and she manages it through
argument, paperwork and flat refusal rather than a fast draw.

You have no patience for being managed, so you negotiate, you check the details and you
turn up exactly when you said you would.

True Grit is the rare Western where the moral centre is the youngest person on screen
and every adult around her has to catch up.

You would get what you came for, and the film is honest about what that takes out of
you.

His new Western drama, The Weight, is probably headed down the same path. The movie debuted in more than 1,500 theaters domestically on September 18, but as of this past weekend, it is playing in only 21 theaters nationwide. The Weight holds a "Certified Fresh" 94% score on Rotten Tomatoes, where the consensus reads, "The Weight turns a stripped-down tale of desperation into a gripping, hard-hitting thriller, elevated by Ethan Hawke's magnetic performance and Padraic McKinley's assured direction." This is the best Rotten Tomatoes rating that one of Crowe's movies has received since Michael Mann's acclaimed thriller The Insider, which now holds a 96% score. The film is likely to find an audience as time passes, especially with McKinley having recently been announced as the director of the upcoming Sicario 3.

Senior Music Editor at Screen Rant, Sarah's love of sound and story drive the beat. A globetrotting brand whisperer and award-winning journalist, she’s built cross-cultural narratives around the world—but music has always been her true north. She launched DJ Mag North America, successfully introducing the iconic UK brand to the U.S. market. Previously, she carved a space for EDM inside the pages of VIBE, blending electronic and hip-hop culture long before it was trendy.

The West Wing could make a meeting about budget negotiations feel as tense as a hostage crisis. Aaron Sorkin's dialogue certainly helped, but so did the conviction that decisions made behind closed doors mattered—and that the people making them might actually care about getting things right.

Across seven seasons, President Josiah "Jed" Bartlet (Martin Sheen) and his exceptionally talented staff navigated political scandals, national emergencies, and the daily absurdities of running the White House. Along the way, viewers became invested in everything from Josh Lyman's disastrous romantic instincts to C.J. Cregg's ability to handle practically any question thrown at her.

Even after The West Wing's celebrated series finale, its particular brand of political storytelling has remained difficult to replace. Plenty of movies feature presidents and politicians, but relatively few capture the exhausting negotiations and personal sacrifices that make public service such compelling drama.

For the closest cinematic equivalent, there's The American President, written by Sorkin four years before The West Wing premiered. Other films, including Thirteen Days and Lincoln, demonstrate how political decisions can become genuinely gripping when filmmakers focus on the people arguing behind closed doors.

Some of these selections are considerably more cynical than Bartlet's White House, while others embrace the same optimism that made the show so beloved. Whether it's the rapid-fire dialogue, complicated relationships, or fascination with how Washington works, these 10 movies offer something for anyone still missing The West Wing.

The American President (1995)

If The West Wing has a cinematic predecessor, it's undoubtedly The American President. Written by Aaron Sorkin and directed by Rob Reiner, the romantic comedy stars Michael Douglas as widowed President Andrew Shepherd, whose budding relationship with environmental lobbyist Sydney Ellen Wade (Annette Bening) threatens his reelection prospects. As their romance becomes a political liability, Shepherd must decide whether protecting his career matters more than standing by the woman he loves.

The similarities to The West Wing extend far beyond Sorkin's recognizable dialogue. Martin Sheen plays White House Chief of Staff A.J. MacInerney, while Michael J. Fox portrays an outspoken domestic policy adviser. The film's combination of sharp political arguments and personal vulnerability would later become central to Sorkin's television series. Among Aaron Sorkin's many movies, this remains the most natural recommendation for Bartlet administration loyalists.

Dave (1993)

Ivan Reitman's Dave offers another appealing vision of the American presidency, albeit through a considerably more improbable premise. Kevin Kline plays Dave Kovic, an ordinary employment agency owner whose resemblance to President Bill Mitchell makes him an ideal temporary stand-in. When the real president suffers a debilitating stroke, White House officials secretly arrange for Dave to continue impersonating him, expecting their substitute to remain easily controlled.

Unfortunately for the conspirators, Dave begins taking his responsibilities seriously. His growing concern for ordinary Americans and his attempts to challenge questionable policies turn the movie into a surprisingly warm political comedy. Sigourney Weaver is especially good as First Lady Ellen Mitchell, who gradually recognizes that the man impersonating her husband possesses qualities the actual president nev er demonstrated. Like The West Wing, Dave imagines how much could change if the people holding power genuinely wanted to help.

Primary Colors (1998)

Mike Nichols' Primary Colors takes audiences inside a presidential campaign that bears an unmistakable resemblance to Bill Clinton's rise to national prominence. John Travolta stars as Southern Governor Jack Stanton, whose extraordinary charisma is matched by his frustrating inability to avoid personal scandals. Adrian Lester plays Henry Burton, an idealistic young campaign adviser who becomes increasingly conflicted about the compromises required to help Stanton win.

The film's ensemble includes Emma Thompson as Stanton's politically astute wife, Susan, and Kathy Bates as the fiercely devoted campaign operative Libby Holden. Adapted from Joe Klein's novel, Primary Colors understands that successful political campaigns depend upon far more than the candidate. Its depiction of exhausted staffers navigating impossible ethical decisions should feel familiar to viewers who watched Josh Lyman and Toby Ziegler wrestle with similar dilemmas. It's also among cinema's most memorable election movies.

The Ides Of March (2011)

George Clooney's The Ides of March offers a far less optimistic examination of campaign politics. Ryan Gosling stars as Stephen Meyers, a talented young press secretary working for presidential hopeful Mike Morris (Clooney). Stephen believes his candidate represents a genuine opportunity to change the country, but a series of betrayals gradually exposes the ruthless calculations behind the campaign's carefully managed public image.

The movie's exceptional supporting cast includes Philip Seymour Hoffman, Paul Giamatti, and Evan Rachel Wood, whose characters complicate Stephen's increasingly desperate attempts to remain politically relevant. Where The West Wing often celebrates the possibility of principled leadership, The Ides of March explores what happens when ambition overwhelms those principles. Gosling's transformation from idealistic strategist into calculating political operator makes the movie a particularly effective companion to Sorkin's more hopeful vision of Washington.

The Contender (2000)

Rod Lurie's The Contender centers on Senator Laine Hanson (Joan Allen), who becomes the president's nominee for vice president following the unexpected death of the previous officeholder. President Jackson Evans (Jeff Bridges) believes Hanson is qualified for the position, but her confirmation process becomes increasingly vicious when political opponents uncover allegations concerning her private life.

Gary Oldman delivers a suitably intimidating performance as Congressman Sheldon Runyon, who leads the effort to discredit Hanson. The movie's most compelling conflict concerns her refusal to dignify invasive questions about her personal history, even when answering them might rescue her nomination. Like the best political thrillers, The Contender recognizes that questions of character and political expediency rarely have simple answers. Its White House confrontations and moral arguments make it especially appealing to West Wing fans.

Thirteen Days (2000)

Few historical events demonstrate the enormous pressure of presidential decision-making as effectively as the Cuban Missile Crisis. Roger Donaldson's Thirteen Days dramatizes the 1962 confrontation between the United States and Soviet Union, with Bruce Greenwood portraying President John F. Kennedy and Steven Culp playing his brother, Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy. Kevin Costner stars as presidential adviser Kenneth O'Donnell, who witnesses the increasingly desperate negotiations.

Much of the film unfolds in government offices, where military leaders and civilian officials argue over responses that could trigger nuclear war. The discussions are tense precisely because the consequences are almost unimaginable, and the president must weigh conflicting advice from people with vastly different priorities. While the historical accuracy of presidential movies varies considerably, Thirteen Days effectively captures the terrifying responsibility of making decisions under extraordinary pressure.

Lincoln (2012)

Steven Spielberg's Lincoln makes the passage of legislation as dramatic as any military confrontation. Daniel Day-Lewis stars as President Abraham Lincoln during the final months of the Civil War, when he is determined to secure congressional approval for the 13th Amendment abolishing slavery. Although his ultimate objective is clear, achieving it requires persuading reluctant lawmakers and navigating political divisions within his own party.

Tony Kushner's screenplay emphasizes negotiations, competing priorities, and the practical difficulties of turning moral convictions into public policy. Day-Lewis gives Lincoln a combination of warmth and political shrewdness that makes his presidency feel remarkably human. The film also acknowledges the historical complexities surrounding the amendment's passage. Anyone who enjoyed watching Bartlet and his staff fight for legislation against seemingly impossible odds should find plenty to appreciate here.

All The President's Men (1976)

Alan J. Pakula's All the President's Men approaches Washington politics from outside the White House, following the journalists whose investigation exposed the Watergate scandal. Robert Redford and Dustin Hoffman portray Washington Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein, who begin examining what initially appears to be a relatively minor burglary before uncovering connections to President Richard Nixon's administration.

Rather than relying upon elaborate action sequences, the film finds tension in telephone conversations, reluctant sources, and the painstaking process of verifying information. Jason Robards is particularly memorable as editor Ben Bradlee, whose demanding leadership helps turn the investigation into a defining moment in American journalism. The movie's reputation as one of the great investigative journalism films is well deserved. Its emphasis on accountability also connects with The West Wing's ongoing examination of political power.

The Trial Of The Chicago 7 (2020)

Aaron Sorkin returned to political history with The Trial of the Chicago 7, which he wrote and directed. Based on the prosecution of anti-Vietnam War protesters following the 1968 Democratic National Convention, the film features an ensemble including Eddie Redmayne, Sacha Baron Cohen, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, and Mark Rylance. Their characters face a deeply contentious trial that becomes a confrontation over civil liberties and government authority.

The courtroom provides an ideal setting for Sorkin's famously energetic dialogue, with political arguments unfolding through heated exchanges and competing interpretations of justice. As with The West Wing, the characters are deeply invested in their convictions, even when those beliefs bring them into conflict with their own allies. Although the screenplay takes significant liberties with the historical events, the film's combination of ensemble performances and political debate makes it an appealing recommendation for Sorkin enthusiasts.

Charlie Wilson's War (2007)

Mike Nichols' Charlie Wilson's War brings Aaron Sorkin's unmistakable writing style into the world of international diplomacy. Tom Hanks stars as real-life Texas Congressman Charlie Wilson, whose interest in supporting Afghan resistance fighters during the Soviet-Afghan War develops into an increasingly ambitious covert operation. Julia Roberts plays influential socialite Joanne Herring, while Philip Seymour Hoffman steals numerous scenes as foul-mouthed CIA operative Gust Avrakotos.

The film's greatest pleasure comes from watching its unlikely collaborators navigate Washington's political machinery. Wilson must secure funding and build relationships across the government while attempting to influence a conflict thousands of miles away. Sorkin gives the process the kind of energy that made ordinary policy disputes so entertaining on The West Wing. The story also examines the consequences of political victories that aren't supported by long-term planning, making this one of the most fascinating Cold War movies told from behind the scenes.

blocks.x: Mike Nichols' Charlie Wilson's War brings Aaron Sorkin's unmistakable writing style into the world of international diplomacy. Tom Hanks stars as real-life Texas Congressman Charlie Wilson, whose interest in supporting Afghan resistance fighters during the Soviet-Afghan War develops into an increasingly ambitious covert operation. Julia Roberts plays influential socialite Joanne Herring, while Philip Seymour Hoffman steals numerous scenes as foul-mouthed CIA operative Gust Avrakotos.

The film's greatest pleasure comes from watching its unlikely collaborators navigate Washington's political machinery. Wilson must secure funding and build relationships across the government while attempting to influence a conflict thousands of miles away. Sorkin gives the process the kind of energy that made ordinary policy disputes so entertaining on The West Wing. The story also examines the consequences of political victories that aren't supported by long-term planning, making this one of the most fascinating Cold War movies told from behind the scenes.

items.text:
If the week had a favorite child, this would be it. Jupiter’s sextile to the Sun reaches its peak, and the Sagittarius Moon trines Jupiter too, so optimism and abundance are practically spilling over. Big asks and long shots have a much better chance than usual, stargazer. By evening, the Sun sextiles the Moon, so what you want and what you need finally agree. Two drawn-out squabbles in the sky come to an end as well, with Pluto releasing Mars from its opposition and Mars ending its square to Mercury. Saturn and Mars hit their peak trine tomorrow, while Pluto turns direct. Go ahead and ask the universe for a little more.

Read your horoscope for the week, and see what the stars have in store for your sign today.

Aries: March 21 – April 19

Long-running feuds eventually bore you to tears. Whoever started it, you’re ready to move on. Pluto’s opposition to Mars and Mars’s square to Mercury both end today, so the power struggle and the bickering lose steam, Aries. Saturn’s trine to Mars peaks tomorrow, pointing your fire toward goals instead of grudges. Extend an olive branch. Peace looks good on a warrior.

Aries monthly horoscope

Taurus: April 20 – May 20

Old passions have a funny way of resurfacing. Maybe it’s the guitar collecting dust or the paint set you swore you’d use again, Taurus. Venus is retrograde, pulling past pleasures back into view, and Pluto’s building square adds an all-or-nothing intensity. Mars is finally letting Venus off the hook, so you won’t need to force it. Give it twenty minutes tonight. Joy counts as productive.

Taurus monthly horoscope

Gemini: May 21 – June 20

Conversation is a two-way street, and you might be hogging both lanes. Jupiter’s square to Mercury keeps your stories coming, Gemini. With the Sagittarius Moon opposite your sign, someone has a tale of their own to tell. Mars’s square to Mercury ends today, so the urge to interrupt fades. Ask a follow-up question and let them run with it. Great talkers make better listeners.

Gemini monthly horoscope

Cancer: June 21 – July 22

For a few hours today, let someone else do the caretaking. You’re always the one checking on everybody, Cancer, so help from others might feel awkward. The Moon trines Jupiter, opening the door to generous gestures, and its sextile with the Sun keeps your heart and head on the same page. Say yes when someone offers. You make a lovely guest of honor.

Cancer monthly horoscope

Leo: July 23 – August 22

Lucky you. Jupiter’s sextile to the Sun peaks today, and fortune seems to follow you around, Leo. A last-minute invite or a surprise upgrade could pop up out of nowhere. Keep your evening wide open. The Sun also sextiles the Moon in adventurous Sagittarius, so excitement sounds irresistible. Say yes before you overthink it. Main characters don’t wait for permission.

Leo monthly horoscope

Virgo: August 23 – September 22

That brain of yours hasn’t had a day off in ages. Mercury’s square with Jupiter keeps piling on new thoughts, Virgo, but the Mars-Mercury square wraps up today, so the mental treadmill finally slows. Take a long walk with no headphones in. Let your mind wander wherever it wants. Some of your best ideas arrive when you stop chasing them.

Virgo monthly horoscope

Libra: September 23 – October 22

“Sure, sounds fun!” has signed you up for a lot of plans you dreaded. Pluto’s square to Venus is building, making it harder to ignore what you want, Libra. Mars and Venus are nearly done sparring, so a polite no won’t start a war. Luckily, the Sun in your sign sextiles Jupiter, adding charm to the delivery. Decline graciously. Your free time is precious.

Libra monthly horoscope

Scorpio: October 23 – November 21

Back in the spring, you were wrestling with questions you couldn’t answer yet. Pluto has been retrograde ever since, doing slow renovation work on your inner world, Scorpio. Tomorrow it turns direct, and its opposition to Mars ends today, so the internal tug-of-war eases. Some answers make sense now. Take a minute to admire how far you’ve come. Growth doesn’t always look flashy.

Scorpio monthly horoscope

Sagittarius: November 22 – December 21

Every so often, someone calls you “a lot,” as if that’s a bad thing. The Moon in your sign trines Jupiter while Jupiter’s sextile to the Sun peaks, so your big energy is a gift, Sagittarius. The right people find your enthusiasm magnetic. Jupiter’s square to Mercury might make you second-guess a comment or two. Let it go. Stay at full volume.

Sagittarius monthly horoscope

Capricorn: December 22 – January 19

Anyone who doubted your side hustle is in for a surprise. Saturn and Mars are a day away from their peak trine, so your drive to push the project forward is at full strength, Capricorn. Uranus’s sextile to Saturn sparks a creative fix for whatever has been holding you back. With Saturn retrograde, lean on lessons from past attempts. Put in the hours tonight.

Capricorn monthly horoscope

Aquarius: January 20 – February 18

At your next outing, someone will ask what you do, and the one-line answer will feel impossible. Neat little labels never fit you anyway, Aquarius. Uranus is retrograde, encouraging you to define yourself on your own terms, and its sextile with Mars lets you answer creatively. Try something unexpected, like your favorite obsession instead of your job title. Mysterious works for you.

Aquarius monthly horoscope

Pisces: February 19 – March 20

Nothing says romance like ink on actual paper. A handwritten note to someone you adore could mean the world to them, Pisces. Romantic or platonic, it counts. Neptune is retrograde, bringing feelings you’ve tucked away back to the surface. Jupiter, your old-school ruler, is radiating luck and generosity today, so your words will be received warmly. Skip the spellcheck. Write from the heart.

Pisces monthly horoscope

items.author: Partner Content With Enshrouded

items.text:
Cozy taverns hidden underwater, whimsical treehouses towering over forests, sprawling cathedrals that took hundreds of hours to make. While some games ask you to discover the worlds other people built, Enshrouded invited players to make it their own. Now the real journey is about to begin.

The folks who played Enshrouded during Early Access already know the wait has been worth it. The long-anticipated 1.0 release, scheduled for October 15, will finally take the game’s ambitious blend of survival RPG and world crafting sim to the next level. The full release promises answers to burning questions about the origins of the Shroud, a poisonous mist that blankets the land, and what led to the fall of Embervale. It also teases new enemies, biomes, and gameplay improvements.

Your task in Enshrouded is to reclaim a kingdom. Embervale has been consumed by the Shroud, a deadly fog that drains your life force and will eventually kill you. The fallen kingdom is a playground of risk and reward, daring players to risk their lives to find powerful treasures. Ancient ruins, hidden cultures, and secrets scattered across a handcrafted world sit beyond the Shroud. Surviving long enough to discover them requires using grappling hooks, gliders, and nail-biting feats of stubbornness to safely navigate the miasma before you run out of time.

Nothing’s random in Enshrouded—everything was put somewhere on purpose. It’s dangerous to try to complete your task alone. Thankfully, you don’t have to.

See at Keen Games

Team Up and Explore

Up to sixteen players on PC, eight players on PS5, can share a world at once, and not everyone has to be toiling away on the same challenge. One player can build and another can explore while a third farms for resources, each contributing to the broader goal of reclaiming Embervale. There is no role in an Enshrouded co-op session that operates outside the loop. As a result, no player has to abandon what they enjoy doing to support someone else’s preferred approach.

That extends to how the game handles its survival systems: hunting, fishing, animal husbandry, and farming all sit alongside combat as ways to obtain resources and upgrades. A player who wants to spend a session cultivating plants and taming animals rather than clearing ruins is playing the game, not working around it.

The PS5 launch that accompanies 1.0 brings a new wave of players into these shared worlds, and a post-launch roadmap means the release is as much a fresh beginning as a well-earned victory lap.

The World Is Yours

While survival games can be harsh and inhospitable, Enshrouded’s brutal world is softened by its cozy sim impulses. It’s an action-RPG for people who might accidentally spend most of their time building pirate ships in a lagoon or a safe fortress at the top of a steep cliff. The world is fully terraformable, which means players aren’t limited to placing pre-made objects on flat ground. Bases can go under waterfalls, inside mountains, and even expand into miniature cities.

Dynamic water was one of the features added during Early Access, a technical feat for a voxel-based game that opened up a new tier of what construction here can look like. Precision tools and pre-made blocks sit at opposite ends of the construction spectrum, and players can move between them as they see fit. To date, Enshrouded’s growing community has produced structures that look less like survival-game shelters and more like long-lost architectural wonders.

Recreated real-world castles, underground cities, giant toilets—the game’s adventure sharing means every player’s creation can become fresh content for someone else.

From Building to Buildcrafting

Combat runs on a skill-based system backed by an upgrade tree deep enough to ensure a diverse pool of viable builds and reward tinkering. Greatswords, magic, hybrid archetypes: The specialization options are broad, and the game doesn’t punish players for choosing an unconventional path through the talent system.

Escalating enemies test whatever build you’ve committed to, which means the combat gets harder as your character gets more capable. But players can tune the difficulty based on their preferences. This means a master base builder can experience low-pressure sessions while hardcore combat enthusiasts can ratchet up the challenge to test their abilities.

It’s exactly this type of flexibility that’s helped Enshrouded earn a 87% positive rating on Steam. More than five million users played Enshrouded during its Early Access, setting the foundation for what the game is today. Community feedback from tens of thousands of hours of players crafting, exploring, and fighting to survive has resulted in reworked combat dynamics, performance optimizations, and system overhauls.

Speaking of improvements, the game has released eight major updates over the past two years to address pain points in collaboration with the community. Perhaps the best example of this is Enshrouded’s final boss, the Fell Dragon Youngling. While it proved to be a challenge for players, developers prioritized fine-tuning the climactic encounter to make it truly memorable. In the upcoming release, gliding, fishing, and pets are also getting fan-requested enhancements.

Enshrouded 1.0 is more than just content complete. Just like the players who have been there from day-one, it’s battle-tested. Improved graphics and performance are part of the 1.0 package, alongside the combat and gameplay revisions that came out of that feedback cycle. For anyone who followed Enshrouded through Early Access and held off for the finished version, mark your calendars and get ready for the real adventure.

Enshrouded 1.0 launches on October 15 on PC, PlayStation 5, and PlayStation 5 Pro, with the Xbox Series X|S version planned for spring 2027.

More than five million users played Enshrouded during its Early Access, setting the foundation for what the game is today. Speaking of improvements, the game has released eight major updates over the past two years to address pain points in collaboration with the community. Perhaps the best example of this is Enshrouded’s final boss, the Fell Dragon Youngling. While it proved to be a challenge for players, developers prioritized fine-tuning the climactic encounter to make it truly memorable. In the upcoming release, gliding, fishing, and pets are also getting fan-requested enhancements.

Enshrouded 1.0 is more than just content complete. Just like the players who have been there from day-one, it’s battle-tested. Improved graphics and performance are part of the 1.0 package, alongside the combat and gameplay revisions that came out of that feedback cycle. items.title: Garry’s Mod Creator Says He’s ‘Ashamed’ And ‘Embarrassed’ By The Response To His Latest Project: ‘I’ve Let Everybody Down’
items.author: John Walker
items.summary: Garry Newman, the creator of the bajillion-selling Garry’s Mod, has not held back when reflecting on his studio’s latest release. The atrociously-named s&box
items.text:
Garry Newman, the creator of the bajillion-selling Garry’s Mod, has not held back when reflecting on his studio’s latest release. The atrociously-named s&box (sandbox, see?) was intended to be the spiritual sequel to Garry’s Mod, the 2008 mod for Valve’s Source engine that went on to sell over 25 million copies. Built for Source 2, Facepunch’s s&box was released in April of this year, and was immediately drowned in AI slop and terrible reviews.

Efforts were quickly made to try to fight back against the user-generated AI drivel that was inundating the project, but unfortunately Newman—who is rarely one to find the right side of an argument—went on to add that he didn’t want to ban AI entirely because it’s “a good learning tool and it’s a good productivity tool.” But these adjustments weren’t enough to turn around early feeling about the open source project, which remains stuck on just 47 percent positive reviews on Steam.

Player numbers have been atrocious. While the 20-year-old Garry’s Mod continues to see almost 30,000 people playing simultaneously every day, s&box barely scrapes 500, despite estimates of anywhere between 500,000 and a million sales. Recently, in an attempt to bring in some more players, Facepunch gave s&box (which hurts me to type each time) a free weekend on Steam, and as IXBT Games noticed, this led to Newman’s first outpouring of loathing for the project under a YouTube video’s coverage of the disastrous promotion.

“The launch was shit,” said Newman. “The free weekend was shit.” Blaming its failure to float under the radar for “burnt bridges” (your guess is as good as mine), he added, “We can’t get away from that, we fucked it. We weren’t ready and we fucked it. We know that, you know that, we fucked it.”

These comments have now been followed up by a blog entry on the game’s official site which condemns just about everything about s&box.

“I’ve been rethinking what s&box should look like over the past couple of weeks,” Newman writes. “The platform is not well liked, it doesn’t have good retention. I’m embarrassed by our reviews, I am ashamed. Listening to all the negative feedback, absorbing, taking it seriously and deciding what we should and shouldn’t be doing. It’s not a big secret that it hasn’t been going well.”

The project lead goes on to state that the core mistake has been selling s&box as an “engine and development experience,” forgetting that the people buying it are far more interested in playing. Newman writes:

…We need to do much much better on the game, we need to shift our focus to what players are experiencing, not developers. Part of this focus is drawing our attention to the Sandbox Game. Giving it parity with the Garry’s Mod version and surpassing it. Showing everyone what the engine can do, adding more NPCs, adding vehicles, offering a first class multiplayer experience, supporting addons and customization. This is a relatively easy task – but I’ve let everyone down that was expecting that. I accept that, and I’m sorry – we are going to do better.

Acknowledging that AI slop is still making it hard for people to find interesting games to download and play within the sandbox, Newman says, “My idea of a Netflix for games doesn’t work. It’s not feasible. It’s not how people discover games.” The intention now is to move away from a sprawling menu of confusing choices, and instead to allow curation to float the best ideas to the top. As Newman puts it, “Where good taste and great opinions are valued beyond everything else. This is a very human thing, this isn’t something that can be replaced by AI, ever.”

The article then goes on to say that the development of Facepunch’s own backend has “mostly been a waste of time and resources,” and he instead intends to shift everything over to the Steam Workshop that was already there, already offering the same service.

And finally, the game is going from $10 to “free to play” before the end of the year. “It’s been pointed out that we are charging for access and also have skins for sale. I don’t think that’s too unusual nowadays, but I can totally understand how combined with everything else that it’s a big turn off. We don’t need the entrance fee, we need players.” Those who already paid will get “a bunch of exclusive steam inventory items…that I hope will justify the purchase price.”

Newman concludes,

I love seeing people create things, I love this engine, and I love working on it. The negative reviews hurt me. The disdain for the project hurts me. I don’t like letting people down, especially when they’ve given me money to provide a service. I understand it all and we’re making some big sweeping changes to try to improve things. Please bear with us while we make these changes.

It’s quite the extraordinary mea culpa, and it’ll be interesting if there’s anything that can turn around the fate of s&box at this stage, after such a terrible launch and bewilderingly small player numbers.
